My recommendation is not to enable all the tested settings. Two-update reuse offers a substantial speed gain, but its quality tradeoff remains unresolved. Liger and sleep mode have correctness problems in the installed stack that prevent recommending them as they stand.

The [full analysis and reproducible evidence](/Users/mheidebrecht/Documents/Projects/Uni/Master_Thesis/master-thesis-code/pipeline/runs/probe_p2_findings.md) are saved.

| Setting | Observed time per update | Matched training reward difference | Recommendation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Baseline | 415 seconds | Reference | Retain for now |
| Liger | 4.8% less time | +1.38 percentage points | Resolve loss mismatch before adoption |
| Two updates per rollout batch | 35.2% less time | -1.63 percentage points* | Promising, but needs quality validation |
| Sleep mode + larger memory allocation | 2.8% more time | -12.44 percentage points | Leave disabled |

*Reuse is compared with the baseline's first 25 generation batches, which cover the same questions.*

All four runs completed their 50 updates. However, none has a held-out evaluation, and everything below comes from one seed.

Liger's apparent success conceals a change in the training objective.

Its training reward is broadly comparable with the baseline: 22 matched batches improve, 20 worsen, and eight tie. That does not establish equivalence.

The source audit found something more decisive. The baseline normalizes its loss using the total active tokens across the accumulated batch. The Liger integration omits that batch total and instead normalizes each individual trajectory before averaging. With our micro-batch size of one, this changes the relative influence of long and short trajectories. It changes gradients, not merely the displayed loss. I verified the missing argument in the installed code and checked an algebraic example demonstrating the different derivatives. [TRL loss implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/blob/v1.6.0/trl/trainer/grpo_trainer.py), [Liger normalization](https://github.com/linkedin/Liger-Kernel/blob/v0.8.2/src/liger_kernel/chunked_loss/fused_linear_ppo.py).

The measured behavior supports taking that discrepancy seriously:

- On the first batch, logged reward and length summaries match, but Liger's gradient norm differs by 26%.
- Across training, Liger's mean gradient norm is 30% higher.
- Its average completion length falls 17%; in the final ten updates, completions are 45% shorter than the baseline.

That shortening matters especially for a thesis studying length rewards. A supposedly neutral implementation setting is already changing how length enters optimization.

It also complicates the speed claim: Liger is slower early, then becomes faster as its outputs shorten. We cannot attribute the full saving to kernel efficiency. Neither memory savings nor 16k feasibility were measured.

My recommendation is to prioritize correcting and validating Liger if the longer context budget is needed. The current run is useful diagnostic evidence, but it fails the equivalence gate.

Sleep mode has the strongest evidence against adoption.

The tested configuration is slightly slower and loses on 42 of 50 matched batches. Its reward deficit grows: over the final ten updates, training reward averages 56.25%, versus 80% for the baseline.

The sampler also increasingly disagrees with the model being trained. By the final update, their mean absolute log-probability difference is about ten times the baseline's.

The installed source provides a concrete explanation: TRL synchronizes the trained weights into vLLM, then the sleep-mode generation path calls `reload_weights` without supplying those updated weights. The installed vLLM implementation consequently reloads the original model from disk. That overwrites the synchronized policy before sampling. [TRL generation implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/blob/v1.6.0/trl/generation/vllm_generation.py), [vLLM weight loading](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.19.1/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py).

This is a source-backed explanation consistent with the logs; the completed run did not record weight checksums that would prove it directly at runtime. It argues against this implementation, not against every correctly implemented sleep mode.

The arm also changed memory utilization from 0.3 to 0.6, so it does not isolate sleep alone. Given the correctness issue and absence of a measured speed benefit, I would spend no further GPU time on it unless memory requirements make it necessary.

Two-update reuse deserves consideration, but the saving needs the right denominator.

It reduced total trainer runtime by about two hours. A generation update averaged 439 seconds; the following reuse update averaged 99 seconds.

But those 50 updates consumed only:

- 100 fresh questions and 800 generated rollouts, versus
- 200 fresh questions and 1,600 rollouts for the baseline.

We bought cheaper optimizer updates by reusing experience. We have not demonstrated faster learning.

On matching questions, reward is 58.25% versus 59.88%. The uncertainty is too wide to establish either a meaningful loss or acceptable equivalence. There are also warning signals: matched mean completion length increases about 11%, and the logged clipped-completion fraction rises from 2.88% to 8.63%. Gradients and sampling corrections otherwise look stable.

I would retain one update as the conservative choice. Reuse is the strongest candidate for further testing if training time is the constraint, using held-out success and an acceptable quality-loss margin chosen before testing.

One additional finding affects the entire setup.

All four probes actually ran with `scale_rewards=group`. The planned campaign uses `scale_rewards=none`. Setting `naive_sum` did not disable the subsequent group scaling.

Therefore, these runs do not validate the final campaign recipe. They also never tested the settings together. We cannot combine their individual gains into an expected result for an all-settings configuration.

The scientific review consequently separates observed performance from correctness and final-policy quality. The report includes paired statistics, dependence-sensitive uncertainty checks, source evidence, and explicit limits.

I removed completed analysis work from `BACKLOG.md` and updated task tracking. Repository checks passed, with three tests skipped; the saved analysis reproduces exactly. Defaults remain unchanged.

Next steps:

- Your decision: proceed with the conservative baseline, or prioritize Liger correction and validation to pursue 16k.
- Keep reuse as an optional quality-versus-time test; leave sleep disabled.
- Freeze the chosen recipe explicitly, then run the E1 pilot and held-out/shifted evaluation.
